nodes.name: Peano System
nodes.question: State the definition: Peano System.
nodes.statement_display:
A triple $(P,S,1)$ is called a \emph{Peano system} exactly when $P$ is a set,
$1 \in P$, $S : P \to P$ is a function, and the following axioms hold:
- $1 \in P$.
- For every $n \in P$, $S(n) \in P$.
- For every $n \in P$, $S(n) \neq 1$.
- For all $m,n \in P$, if $S(m)=S(n)$ then $m=n$.
- If $A \subseteq P$, $1 \in A$, and
 \[
 \forall n \in P\;(n \in A \Longrightarrow S(n) \in A),
 \]
 then $A=P$.
nodes.statement_tex:
A triple $(P,S,1)$ is called a \emph{Peano system} exactly when $P$ is a set,
$1 \in P$, $S : P \to P$ is a function, and the following axioms hold:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item[\textbf{P1.}] $1 \in P$.
 \item[\textbf{P2.}] For every $n \in P$, $S(n) \in P$.
 \item[\textbf{P3.}] For every $n \in P$, $S(n) \neq 1$.
 \item[\textbf{P4.}] For all $m,n \in P$, if $S(m)=S(n)$ then $m=n$.
 \item[\textbf{P5.}] If $A \subseteq P$, $1 \in A$, and
 \[
 \forall n \in P\;(n \in A \Longrightarrow S(n) \in A),
 \]
 then $A=P$.
\end{enumerate}
nodes.formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(P,S,1) \text{ is a Peano system}\\
&\Longleftrightarrow
\Bigl(P \text{ is a set} \land 1 \in P \land S : P \to P \\
&\qquad \land \forall n \in P\;(S(n) \in P) \\
&\qquad \land \forall n \in P\;(S(n) \neq 1) \\
&\qquad \land \forall m,n \in P\;(S(m)=S(n) \Longrightarrow m=n) \\
&\qquad \land \forall A \subseteq P\;
\bigl((1 \in A \land
\forall n \in P\;(n \in A \Longrightarrow S(n) \in A))
\Longrightarrow A=P\bigr)\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(P,S,1) \text{ is a Peano system}\\
&\Longleftrightarrow
\Bigl(P \text{ is a set} \land 1 \in P \land S : P \to P \\
&\qquad \land \forall n \in P\;(S(n) \in P) \\
&\qquad \land \forall n \in P\;(S(n) \neq 1) \\
&\qquad \land \forall m,n \in P\;(S(m)=S(n) \Longrightarrow m=n) \\
&\qquad \land \forall A \subseteq P\;
\bigl((1 \in A \land
\forall n \in P\;(n \in A \Longrightarrow S(n) \in A))
\Longrightarrow A=P\bigr)\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.failure_modes:
A triple $(P,S,1)$ fails to be a Peano system if the distinguished element
does not lie in the underlying set, if the successor map leaves the set, if
the successor hits $1$, if the successor identifies two distinct elements, or
if there exists a proper subset of $P$ that contains $1$ and is closed under
successor.
nodes.failure_mode_decomposition:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\neg\,\text{$(P,S,1)$ is a Peano system}
\Longrightarrow\;&
1 \notin P \\
&\lor \exists n \in P\;(S(n) \notin P) \\
&\lor \exists n \in P\;(S(n)=1) \\
&\lor \exists m,n \in P\;(m \neq n \land S(m)=S(n)) \\
&\lor \exists A \subseteq P\;
\bigl(1 \in A \land
\forall n \in P\;(n \in A \Longrightarrow S(n) \in A)
\land A \neq P\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.source_text:
A Peano system is the abstract data of counting: an underlying set, a first
element, and a successor operation satisfying the usual non-collision and
induction principles. The purpose of the definition is to isolate the ambient
object before the individual axioms are recorded and used one by one.

The counting system begins from a distinguished first element of the
underlying set. This is the base point from which the remaining elements are
generated by the successor operation.

closed under successor must already contain the entire set. This axiom rules
out rogue elements and is the logical source of mathematical induction.

nodes.name: Induction Principle for a Peano System
nodes.question: State the theorem: Induction Principle for a Peano System.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $\varphi$ be a predicate on $P$.
If
\[
\varphi(1)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n \in P\;(\varphi(n) \Longrightarrow \varphi(S(n))),
\]
then
\[
\forall n \in P\;\varphi(n).
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $\varphi$ be a predicate on $P$.
If
\[
\varphi(1)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n \in P\;(\varphi(n) \Longrightarrow \varphi(S(n))),
\]
then
\[
\forall n \in P\;\varphi(n).
\]
nodes.formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system and let } \varphi
\text{ be a predicate on } P.\\
&\Bigl(\varphi(1) \land
\forall n \in P\;(\varphi(n) \Longrightarrow \varphi(S(n)))\Bigr)
\Longrightarrow
\forall n \in P\;\varphi(n).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system and let } \varphi
\text{ be a predicate on } P.\\
&\Bigl(\varphi(1) \land
\forall n \in P\;(\varphi(n) \Longrightarrow \varphi(S(n)))\Bigr)
\Longrightarrow
\forall n \in P\;\varphi(n).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.contrapositive:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system and let } \varphi
\text{ be a predicate on } P.\\
&\neg\forall n \in P\;\varphi(n)
\Longrightarrow
\neg\Bigl(\varphi(1) \land
\forall n \in P\;(\varphi(n) \Longrightarrow \varphi(S(n)))\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.proof_sketch:
Step 1. Translate the predicate into a subset. Every predicate $\varphi$ on a set $P$ determines an extension: the set of
elements for which the predicate holds. Define
\[
  A \;\coloneqq\; \{\,n \in P \mid \varphi(n)\,\}.
\]
Since $\varphi$ is a predicate on $P$, the subset $A$ is well-defined as a
subset of $P$, that is, $A \subseteq P$.  

The goal $\forall n \in P\,\varphi(n)$ is now equivalent to $A = P$: every
element of $P$ satisfies $\varphi$ if and only if every element of $P$
belongs to $A$. The proof will establish $A = P$ by applying the induction
axiom.
Step 2. Verify the base condition: $1 \in A$. The first hypothesis is $\varphi(1)$.
By the definition of $A$, $\varphi(1)$ holds if and only if $1 \in A$.
Since $\varphi(1)$ is given, we conclude $1 \in A$.
Step 3. Verify the successor-closure condition. The second hypothesis is
\[
  \forall n \in P\;(\varphi(n) \Longrightarrow \varphi(S(n))).
\]
Let $n \in P$ be arbitrary and suppose $n \in A$.
By the definition of $A$, $n \in A$ means precisely $\varphi(n)$.
The second hypothesis then gives $\varphi(S(n))$.
Since $S(n) \in P$ (by the closure axiom for a Peano system) and
$\varphi(S(n))$ holds, the definition of $A$ gives $S(n) \in A$.

Since $n$ was arbitrary, this establishes
\[
  \forall n \in P\;(n \in A \Longrightarrow S(n) \in A).
\]
The subset $A$ is therefore successor-closed.
Step 4. Conclude that $A$ is an inductive subset. Combining Steps 2 and 3:
\[
  1 \in A
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  \forall n \in P\;(n \in A \Longrightarrow S(n) \in A).
\]
By the definition of an inductive subset
\hyperref[def:inductive-subset-of-peano-system]{(Definition: Inductive Subset of a Peano System)},
$A$ is an inductive subset of the Peano system $(P,S,1)$.
Step 5. Apply the induction axiom. The induction axiom \hyperref[ax:peano-induction]{(P5)} states: any subset
$A \subseteq P$ that contains $1$ and is closed under successor satisfies
$A = P$. Steps 2 and 3 establish exactly these two conditions. Therefore
$A = P$.
Step 6. Conclude the predicate holds universally. Since $A = P$, every element $n \in P$ belongs to $A$. By the definition of
$A$, this means $\varphi(n)$ holds for every $n \in P$. That is,
\[
  \forall n \in P\;\varphi(n). \qedhere
\]
proof_steps:
Step 1. Translate the predicate into a subset. Every predicate $\varphi$ on a set $P$ determines an extension: the set of
elements for which the predicate holds. Define
\[
  A \;\coloneqq\; \{\,n \in P \mid \varphi(n)\,\}.
\]
Since $\varphi$ is a predicate on $P$, the subset $A$ is well-defined as a
subset of $P$, that is, $A \subseteq P$.  

The goal $\forall n \in P\,\varphi(n)$ is now equivalent to $A = P$: every
element of $P$ satisfies $\varphi$ if and only if every element of $P$
belongs to $A$. The proof will establish $A = P$ by applying the induction
axiom.

Step 2. Verify the base condition: $1 \in A$. The first hypothesis is $\varphi(1)$.
By the definition of $A$, $\varphi(1)$ holds if and only if $1 \in A$.
Since $\varphi(1)$ is given, we conclude $1 \in A$.

Step 3. Verify the successor-closure condition. The second hypothesis is
\[
  \forall n \in P\;(\varphi(n) \Longrightarrow \varphi(S(n))).
\]
Let $n \in P$ be arbitrary and suppose $n \in A$.
By the definition of $A$, $n \in A$ means precisely $\varphi(n)$.
The second hypothesis then gives $\varphi(S(n))$.
Since $S(n) \in P$ (by the closure axiom for a Peano system) and
$\varphi(S(n))$ holds, the definition of $A$ gives $S(n) \in A$.

Since $n$ was arbitrary, this establishes
\[
  \forall n \in P\;(n \in A \Longrightarrow S(n) \in A).
\]
The subset $A$ is therefore successor-closed.

Step 4. Conclude that $A$ is an inductive subset. Combining Steps 2 and 3:
\[
  1 \in A
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  \forall n \in P\;(n \in A \Longrightarrow S(n) \in A).
\]
By the definition of an inductive subset
\hyperref[def:inductive-subset-of-peano-system]{(Definition: Inductive Subset of a Peano System)},
$A$ is an inductive subset of the Peano system $(P,S,1)$.

Step 5. Apply the induction axiom. The induction axiom \hyperref[ax:peano-induction]{(P5)} states: any subset
$A \subseteq P$ that contains $1$ and is closed under successor satisfies
$A = P$. Steps 2 and 3 establish exactly these two conditions. Therefore
$A = P$.

Step 6. Conclude the predicate holds universally. Since $A = P$, every element $n \in P$ belongs to $A$. By the definition of
$A$, this means $\varphi(n)$ holds for every $n \in P$. That is,
\[
  \forall n \in P\;\varphi(n). \qedhere
\]
nodes.proof_idea:
The proof is a direct application of the induction axiom (P5). The induction
axiom is formulated in terms of subsets: any inductive subset of $P$ must
equal $P$ itself. The predicate $\varphi$ does not appear in (P5), so the
first move is always to translate --- passing from the predicate form to the
subset form via the extension $A \coloneqq \{\,n \in P \mid \varphi(n)\,\}$.
Once the translation is made, the two hypotheses map exactly onto the two
conditions that (P5) requires: the base condition $1 \in A$ comes from
$\varphi(1)$, and successor-closure of $A$ comes from the step hypothesis on
$\varphi$. The induction axiom then forces $A = P$, and translating back gives
the conclusion.

This translation pattern --- predicate to subset, apply (P5), translate back
--- is the invariant structure of every induction proof in the Peano system
framework.
nodes.source_text:
This theorem converts the subset form of induction into the predicate form
used in ordinary arithmetic arguments. A property propagates through the
entire Peano system once it holds at the distinguished first element and is
preserved by successor. The theorem therefore turns the structural induction
axiom into a proof principle for arbitrary predicates on $P$.

\forall n \in P\;(n \in A \Longrightarrow S(n) \in A).

nodes.failure_modes:
A subset fails to be successor-closed exactly when it contains some element of
$P$ but fails to contain that element's successor.
nodes.source_text:
A successor-closed subset is stable under one step of counting. Once an
element of $A$ is present, its successor remains in $A$ as well.

Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $A \subseteq P$. The subset $A$ is
called \emph{inductive} exactly when $1 \in A$ and $A$ is successor-closed.
nodes.failure_modes:
A subset fails to be inductive in exactly two ways: it may fail to contain the
distinguished first element, or it may contain some element while failing to
contain that element's successor.
nodes.source_text:
An inductive subset contains the distinguished first element and is closed
under successor. Such a subset contains every stage obtained by starting at
$1$ and applying successor repeatedly.

nodes.name: Every Element Is Either $1$ or a Successor
nodes.question: State the theorem: Every Element Is Either $1$ or a Successor.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $x \in P$, either $x=1$ or there
exists $u \in P$ such that $S(u)=x$.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $x \in P$, either $x=1$ or there
exists $u \in P$ such that $S(u)=x$.
nodes.proof_sketch:
\textbf{Professional Standard Proof.}~\\
Let
\[
D:=\{x\in P:x=1 \text{ or } \exists u\in P\;(S(u)=x)\}.
\]
We show that $D$ is inductive. Since $1=1$, we have $1\in D$.

Now let $x\in D$. By closure of successor, $S(x)\in P$. Moreover $x\in P$,
so $S(x)$ is the successor of an element of $P$. Hence $S(x)\in D$.
Therefore $D$ contains $1$ and is closed under successor. By the induction
principle, $D=P$.

Thus every $x\in P$ lies in $D$, so every $x\in P$ satisfies either $x=1$ or
there exists $u\in P$ such that $S(u)=x$.
nodes.proof_idea:
The proof forms the subset of all elements satisfying the desired dichotomy
and then proves that this subset is inductive. The base case is immediate
from $1=1$. The successor step is immediate because every successor is, by
definition, a successor of an element of $P$.
nodes.source_text:
Every element of a Peano system is reached by starting at the distinguished
first element and moving forward by successor. The only possible exception to
having a predecessor is the element $1$ itself.

nodes.name: Successor Inequality Reflection
nodes.question: State the theorem: Successor Inequality Reflection.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For all $a,b \in P$, if $a \neq b$, then
$S(a)\neq S(b)$.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For all $a,b \in P$, if $a \neq b$, then
$S(a)\neq S(b)$.
nodes.failure_modes:
Successor inequality reflection fails exactly when two distinct elements have
the same successor.
nodes.source_text:
The successor operation reflects inequality: distinct inputs remain distinct
after one successor step. This is the contrapositive form of successor
injectivity, and it is the form used when an induction step must preserve a
negative equality statement.

nodes.name: Predecessor Existence and Uniqueness Away from $1$
nodes.question: State the corollary: Predecessor Existence and Uniqueness Away from $1$.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $x \in P$ with $x \neq 1$. Then
there exists a unique $u \in P$ such that $S(u)=x$.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $x \in P$ with $x \neq 1$. Then
there exists a unique $u \in P$ such that $S(u)=x$.
nodes.proof_sketch:
\textbf{Professional Standard Proof.}~\\
By
\hyperref[thm:every-element-is-one-or-a-successor]{Every Element Is Either
$1$ or a Successor}, either $x=1$ or there exists $u\in P$ such that
$S(u)=x$. Since $x\neq 1$, the first alternative is impossible. Hence there
exists $u\in P$ such that $S(u)=x$.

To prove uniqueness, let $v\in P$ and suppose $S(v)=x$. Since also $S(u)=x$,
we have
\[
S(v)=S(u).
\]
By injectivity of the successor map, $v=u$. Therefore there exists a unique
$u\in P$ such that $S(u)=x$.
nodes.proof_idea:
Existence comes from the dichotomy theorem after ruling out the case $x=1$.
Uniqueness is a direct application of injectivity of the successor map: two
elements with the same successor must be equal.
nodes.source_text:
Every element distinct from $1$ has exactly one predecessor. The successor map
therefore organizes the non-initial part of a Peano system into one-step
extensions of earlier elements.
depends_on_titles: The Distinguished Element Is the Unique Non-Successor

nodes.name: Unique Predecessor Characterization Away from $1$
nodes.question: State the corollary: Unique Predecessor Characterization Away from $1$.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $x \in P$, $x \neq 1$ if and
only if there exists a unique $u \in P$ such that $S(u)=x$.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $x \in P$, $x \neq 1$ if and
only if there exists a unique $u \in P$ such that $S(u)=x$.
nodes.formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system.}\\
&\forall x \in P\;\bigl(x\neq 1 \Longleftrightarrow
\exists! u \in P\;(S(u)=x)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system.}\\
&\forall x \in P\;\bigl(x\neq 1 \Longleftrightarrow
\exists! u \in P\;(S(u)=x)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.negation_display:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system.}\\
&\exists x \in P\;\Bigl(
\bigl(x\neq 1 \land
(\forall u \in P\;(S(u)\neq x)\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\lor
\exists u,v \in P\;(S(u)=x \land S(v)=x \land u\neq v))\bigr)\\
&\qquad\qquad\lor
\bigl(x=1 \land \exists u \in P\;(S(u)=x \land
\forall v \in P\;(S(v)=x \Longrightarrow v=u))\bigr)
\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.negation_formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system.}\\
&\exists x \in P\;\Bigl(
\bigl(x\neq 1 \land
(\forall u \in P\;(S(u)\neq x)\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\lor
\exists u,v \in P\;(S(u)=x \land S(v)=x \land u\neq v))\bigr)\\
&\qquad\qquad\lor
\bigl(x=1 \land \exists u \in P\;(S(u)=x \land
\forall v \in P\;(S(v)=x \Longrightarrow v=u))\bigr)
\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.failure_modes:
The biconditional can fail in two ways: a non-initial element can fail to have
a unique predecessor, or the distinguished first element can have a unique
predecessor.
nodes.failure_mode_decomposition:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\exists x \in P\;\Bigl(
\underbrace{\bigl(x\neq 1 \land
(\forall u \in P\;(S(u)\neq x)
\lor
\exists u,v \in P\;(S(u)=x \land S(v)=x \land u\neq v))\bigr)}_
{\text{non-initial element lacks a unique predecessor}}\\
&\qquad\qquad\lor
\underbrace{\bigl(x=1 \land \exists u \in P\;(S(u)=x \land
\forall v \in P\;(S(v)=x \Longrightarrow v=u))\bigr)}_
{\text{the first element has a unique predecessor}}
\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.source_text:
Being different from the distinguished first element is exactly the same as
having a unique predecessor. This turns the informal phrase "away from $1$"
into an internal characterization of the successor structure.

nodes.name: The Distinguished Element Is the Unique Non-Successor
nodes.question: State the corollary: The Distinguished Element Is the Unique Non-Successor.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. An element $x \in P$ is not a successor of
any element of $P$ if and only if $x=1$.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. An element $x \in P$ is not a successor of
any element of $P$ if and only if $x=1$.
nodes.proof_sketch:
\textbf{Professional Standard Proof.}~\\
Assume first that $x\in P$ is not a successor of any element of $P$. By
\hyperref[thm:every-element-is-one-or-a-successor]{Every Element Is Either
$1$ or a Successor}, either $x=1$ or there exists $u\in P$ such that
$S(u)=x$. The second alternative contradicts the assumption that $x$ is not a
successor. Hence $x=1$.

Conversely, suppose $x=1$. By the Peano axiom that $1$ is not a successor,
there is no $u\in P$ such that $S(u)=1$. Since $x=1$, there is no $u\in P$
such that $S(u)=x$. Therefore $x$ is not a successor of any element of $P$.
nodes.proof_idea:
The forward implication uses the dichotomy theorem and eliminates the
successor case. The reverse implication is exactly the Peano axiom that the
distinguished element is not a successor.
nodes.source_text:
The distinguished first element is characterized internally as the unique
element with no predecessor. This gives a structural description of $1$ that
does not depend on external notation.

Predecessor Existence and Uniqueness Away from $1$

nodes.name: No Object Is Its Own Successor
nodes.question: State the theorem: No Object Is Its Own Successor.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $n \in P$,
\[
S(n) \neq n.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $n \in P$,
\[
S(n) \neq n.
\]
nodes.proof_sketch:
\textbf{Professional Standard Proof.}~\\
Let
\[
D:=\{x\in P:S(x)\neq x\}.
\]
We prove that $D=P$ by induction.

First, $1\in D$. Indeed, if $S(1)=1$, then $1$ would be the successor of the
element $1\in P$, contradicting the Peano axiom that $1$ is not a successor.
Thus $S(1)\neq 1$.

Now assume $n\in D$. Then $S(n)\neq n$. If $S(S(n))=S(n)$, injectivity of
$S$ would imply $S(n)=n$, contradicting $n\in D$. Therefore
$S(S(n))\neq S(n)$, so $S(n)\in D$.

Thus $D$ contains $1$ and is closed under successor. By the induction
principle, $D=P$. Hence for every $n\in P$, $S(n)\neq n$.
nodes.proof_idea:
The proof uses induction on the subset of elements that are not equal to
their own successors. The base case uses the axiom that $1$ is not a
successor. The successor step uses the contrapositive form of injectivity:
from $S(n)\neq n$, one obtains $S(S(n))\neq S(n)$.
nodes.source_text:
Successor always moves forward in the counting structure. No element can be
recovered by applying successor to itself.
used_by_titles: Distinguished Element Is Not a Successor
Induction Principle for a Peano System

nodes.name: Minimal Iterator Relation
nodes.question: State the definition: Minimal Iterator Relation.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it.
The \emph{minimal iterator relation} for $(W,c,g)$ is
\[
R^*
=
\bigcap\{R\subseteq P\times W : R \text{ is an iterator relation for }
(W,c,g)\}.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it.
The \emph{minimal iterator relation} for $(W,c,g)$ is
\[
R^*
=
\bigcap\{R\subseteq P\times W : R \text{ is an iterator relation for }
(W,c,g)\}.
\]
nodes.proposition:
Let $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{it}}$ be the closure condition
\[
\mathcal C_{\mathrm{it}}(R)
\Longleftrightarrow
\operatorname{IteratorRelation}(R,(P,S,1),W,c,g).
\]
Then the definition says
\[
\operatorname{MinimalRelation}(R^*,\mathcal C_{\mathrm{it}}).
\]
nodes.formal:
\[
(n,w)\in R^*
\Longleftrightarrow
\forall R\subseteq P\times W\;
\bigl(R \text{ is an iterator relation for } (W,c,g)
\Longrightarrow (n,w)\in R\bigr).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
(n,w)\in R^*
\Longleftrightarrow
\forall R\subseteq P\times W\;
\bigl(R \text{ is an iterator relation for } (W,c,g)
\Longrightarrow (n,w)\in R\bigr).
\]
nodes.negation_display:
\[
(n,w)\notin R^*
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists R\subseteq P\times W\;
\bigl(R \text{ is an iterator relation for } (W,c,g)\land (n,w)\notin R\bigr).
\]
nodes.negation_formal:
\[
(n,w)\notin R^*
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists R\subseteq P\times W\;
\bigl(R \text{ is an iterator relation for } (W,c,g)\land (n,w)\notin R\bigr).
\]
nodes.failure_modes:
A pair fails to belong to the minimal iterator relation exactly when some
iterator relation omits that pair. Such a pair is not forced by the base and
successor-closure clauses.
nodes.source_text:
The minimal iterator relation consists exactly of the stage-value pairs forced
by the base pair and the successor closure rule. This is the $R^*$ construction
used in the classical proof strategy
\citep{feferman1964numbersystems,hrbacek_jech1999,chi_recursion_wustl}.

nodes.name: Uniqueness of Iterator Functions
nodes.question: State the lemma: Uniqueness of Iterator Functions.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it. If
$f,h:P\to W$ satisfy
\[
f(1)=c,\qquad h(1)=c,
\]
and
\[
\forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=g(f(n)))
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n\in P\;(h(S(n))=g(h(n))),
\]
then $f=h$.

The iterator clauses determine at most one function. Any difference between
two candidate functions must show up as a failure of the base clause or a
failure of one of the successor clauses.

nodes.name: Existence of an Iterator Function
nodes.question: State the lemma: Existence of an Iterator Function.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it.
Then there exists a function $f:P\to W$ such that
\[
f(1)=c
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=g(f(n))).
\]

Existence fails exactly when every candidate function misses the base value or

\]
nodes.source_text:
Existence is the assertion that the minimal relation is not merely graph-like
locally, but supplies a value at every stage and hence determines an actual
function.

nodes.name: Peano Iterator Theorem
nodes.question: State the theorem: Peano Iterator Theorem.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it.
Then there exists a unique function $f:P\to W$ such that
\[
f(1)=c
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=g(f(n))).
\]

nodes.failure_modes:
The iterator theorem fails only if no function satisfies the iterator clauses
or if more than one function satisfies them.
nodes.source_text:
The theorem says that iterator data is sufficient to turn a recursive
specification into a genuine definition: there is exactly one graph and hence
exactly one function satisfying the base and successor clauses.

nodes.name: Iterator-Generated Function
nodes.question: State the definition: Iterator-Generated Function.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it.
The unique function $f:P\to W$ satisfying
\[
f(1)=c
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=g(f(n)))
\]
is called the \emph{iterator-generated function determined by $(W,c,g)$}.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it.
The unique function $f:P\to W$ satisfying
\[
f(1)=c
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=g(f(n)))
\]
is called the \emph{iterator-generated function determined by $(W,c,g)$}.
nodes.formal:
\[
f \text{ is the iterator-generated function determined by } (W,c,g)
\Longleftrightarrow
\bigl(f:P\to W\land f(1)=c
\land \forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=g(f(n)))\bigr).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:

\Longleftrightarrow
\bigl(f:P\to W\land f(1)=c
\land \forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=g(f(n)))\bigr).
\]

\begin{aligned}
f \text{ is not the iterator-generated function determined by } (W,c,g)
\Longleftrightarrow\;&
f \text{ is not a function } P\to W\\
&\lor f(1)\neq c
\lor \exists n\in P\;(f(S(n))\neq g(f(n))).
\end{aligned}
\]

nodes.failure_modes:
A candidate fails to be the iterator-generated function if it is not a
function from $P$ to $W$, if it has the wrong base value, or if it violates

nodes.name: Uniqueness of Binary Iterator Operations
nodes.question: State the corollary: Uniqueness of Binary Iterator Operations.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $A$ be a set, let $W$ be a set, and
suppose each $a\in A$ determines iterator data $(W,c_a,g_a)$ for $(P,S,1)$.
If $F,G:A\times P\to W$ satisfy
\[
F(a,1)=c_a,\qquad G(a,1)=c_a
\]
and
\[
F(a,S(n))=g_a(F(a,n)),
\qquad
G(a,S(n))=g_a(G(a,n))
\]
for all $a\in A$ and all $n\in P$, then $F=G$.
nodes.statement_tex:

If $F,G:A\times P\to W$ satisfy

\]

\qquad
G(a,S(n))=g_a(G(a,n))
\]

\Longrightarrow F_a=G_a\bigr).

\land G(a,S(n))=g_a(G(a,n))\Bigr)
\Longrightarrow F=G.

nodes.name: Stage-Dependent Step Rule

nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system and let $W$ be a set. A
\emph{stage-dependent step rule} on $W$ over $P$ is a function
\[
\Phi:P\times W\to W.
\]

current Peano stage and the current value.

nodes.name: General Recursive Function
nodes.question: State the definition: General Recursive Function.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $W$ be a set, let $c\in W$, and let
$\Phi:P\times W\to W$ be a stage-dependent step rule. A function $f:P\to W$
is called the \emph{general recursive function determined by $(W,c,\Phi)$}
exactly when
\[
f(1)=c
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=\Phi(n,f(n))).
\]

nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S_P,1_P)$ and $(Q,S_Q,1_Q)$ be Peano systems. Then there exists a
unique bijection $\theta:P\to Q$ such that
\[
\theta(1_P)=1_Q
\]

\]
Thus any two Peano systems are isomorphic.

nodes.statement_display:

function
\[
f_m : P \to P
\]
such that
\[
f_m(1)=S(m)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n \in P\;(f_m(S(n))=S(f_m(n))).
\]
Consequently the rule
\[
(m,n) \longmapsto m+n \coloneqq f_m(n)
\]
defines a unique binary operation on $P$.

right-input map for each fixed left input. The addition operation is therefore
not assumed; it is constructed from the successor map by recursion.

nodes.name: $ $ Is Closed, Associative, and Commutative Under Addition
nodes.question: State the theorem: $ $ Is Closed, Associative, and Commutative Under Addition.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. The binary operation $+$ on $P$ satisfies:
- \textbf{Closure.} For all $a,b \in P$, $a+b \in P$.
- \textbf{Associativity.} For all $a,b,c \in P$,
 $(a+b)+c = a+(b+c)$.
- \textbf{Commutativity.} For all $a,b \in P$, $a+b = b+a$.
- \textbf{Left cancellation.} For all $a,b,c \in P$, if $a+b = a+c$ then $b=c$.
- \textbf{Right cancellation.} For all $a,b,c \in P$, if $b+a = c+a$ then $b=c$.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. The binary operation $+$ on $P$ satisfies:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item \textbf{Closure.} For all $a,b \in P$, $a+b \in P$.
 \item \textbf{Associativity.} For all $a,b,c \in P$,
 $(a+b)+c = a+(b+c)$.
 \item \textbf{Commutativity.} For all $a,b \in P$, $a+b = b+a$.
 \item \textbf{Left cancellation.} For all $a,b,c \in P$, if $a+b = a+c$ then $b=c$.
 \item \textbf{Right cancellation.} For all $a,b,c \in P$, if $b+a = c+a$ then $b=c$.
\end{enumerate}
nodes.source_text:
This theorem is a packaging result. It names the algebraic structure that
has been proved piece by piece: the three individual theorems on associativity,
commutativity, and cancellation together certify that $(P,+)$ is a cancellative
commutative semigroup. There is no additive identity in $P$ because $P$ has
no element $0$ with $0+n=n$ for all $n$; the smallest element under addition
is $1$, not an identity.

nodes.name: $ $ Is a Commutative Monoid Under Multiplication
nodes.question: State the theorem: $ $ Is a Commutative Monoid Under Multiplication.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. The binary operation $\cdot$ on $P$ satisfies:
- \textbf{Closure.} For all $a,b \in P$, $a \cdot b \in P$.
- \textbf{Associativity.} For all $a,b,c \in P$,
 $(a \cdot b) \cdot c = a \cdot (b \cdot c)$.
- \textbf{Commutativity.} For all $a,b \in P$,
 $a \cdot b = b \cdot a$.
- \textbf{Identity.} For all $a \in P$,
 $1 \cdot a = a = a \cdot 1$.
Consequently $(P, \cdot, 1)$ is a commutative monoid.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. The binary operation $\cdot$ on $P$ satisfies:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item \textbf{Closure.} For all $a,b \in P$, $a \cdot b \in P$.
 \item \textbf{Associativity.} For all $a,b,c \in P$,
 $(a \cdot b) \cdot c = a \cdot (b \cdot c)$.
 \item \textbf{Commutativity.} For all $a,b \in P$,
 $a \cdot b = b \cdot a$.
 \item \textbf{Identity.} For all $a \in P$,
 $1 \cdot a = a = a \cdot 1$.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently $(P, \cdot, 1)$ is a commutative monoid.
nodes.source_text:
The distinguished first element $1$ is a multiplicative identity on both
sides, so multiplication promotes $P$ from a semigroup to a monoid. The
absence of multiplicative inverses (other than $1^{-1} = 1$, which does not
lie in $P$ in the usual sense) is what prevents $(P,\cdot)$ from being a
group. The structural limitation is intrinsic: no element of $P$ other than
$1$ has a reciprocal in $P$.

nodes.name: $ $ Is a Semiring
nodes.question: State the theorem: $ $ Is a Semiring.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. Then $(P,+,\cdot)$ satisfies:
- $(P,+)$ is a commutative semigroup.
- $(P,\cdot,1)$ is a commutative monoid.
- Multiplication distributes over addition: for all $a,b,c \in P$,
 \[
 a \cdot (b+c) = (a \cdot b) + (a \cdot c).
 \]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. Then $(P,+,\cdot)$ satisfies:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item $(P,+)$ is a commutative semigroup.
 \item $(P,\cdot,1)$ is a commutative monoid.
 \item Multiplication distributes over addition: for all $a,b,c \in P$,
 \[
 a \cdot (b+c) = (a \cdot b) + (a \cdot c).
 \]
\end{enumerate}
nodes.source_text:
A semiring packages the interaction of two operations without requiring
additive inverses. The natural numbers are the canonical example of a semiring
that is not a ring: they satisfy every ring axiom except the existence of
additive inverses, which fails because there is no element $-1$ in $P$.
The integers are the smallest ring extending $P$ that repairs this failure.

nodes.name: Tao 2.2.12 — Basic properties of order
nodes.question: State the proposition: Tao 2.2.12 — Basic properties of order.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $a, b, c \in \mathbb{N}$.
- \textbf{Reflexive.} $a \geq a$.
- \textbf{Transitive.} If $a \geq b$ and $b \geq c$, then $a \geq c$.
- \textbf{Anti-symmetric.} If $a \geq b$ and $b \geq a$, then $a = b$.
- \textbf{Addition preserves order.}
 $a \geq b \iff a + c \geq b + c$.
- $a < b \iff a\pp \leq b$.
- $a < b \iff b = a + d$ for some positive $d$.

nodes.name: Strong Induction on a Peano System
nodes.question: State the theorem: Strong Induction on a Peano System.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $\varphi$ be a predicate on $P$.
If
\[
\forall n \in P\;
\bigl(\forall k \in P\;(k < n \Longrightarrow \varphi(k))\bigr)
\Longrightarrow \varphi(n),
\]
then
\[
\forall n \in P\;\varphi(n).
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $\varphi$ be a predicate on $P$.
If
\[
\forall n \in P\;
\bigl(\forall k \in P\;(k < n \Longrightarrow \varphi(k))\bigr)
\Longrightarrow \varphi(n),
\]
then
\[
\forall n \in P\;\varphi(n).
\]
nodes.source_text:
Strong induction grants the inductive step access to the entire history below
$n$, not just the single predecessor. The contrapositive gives the least
counterexample principle: if any element fails $\varphi$, there is a least
one, and that least one has $\varphi$ holding at all its predecessors, which
contradicts the strong-induction hypothesis. This makes strong induction and
least-counterexample arguments two descriptions of the same logical structure.

nodes.name: Multiplication Is Well-Defined on a Peano System
nodes.question: State the theorem: Multiplication Is Well-Defined on a Peano System.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $m \in P$, there exists a unique
function
\[
g_m : P \to P
\]
such that
\[
g_m(1)=m
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n \in P\;(g_m(S(n))=g_m(n)+m).
\]
Consequently the rule
\[
(m,n) \longmapsto m \cdot n \coloneqq g_m(n)
\]
defines a unique binary operation on $P$.

constructed from recursion and addition rather than assumed at the outset.

nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $a,b \in P$. One writes
\[

\]

\[
b=a+c.

\[
a<b

\]

&a<b
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists c \in P\;(b=a+c).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system and let } a,b \in P.\\
&a<b
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists c \in P\;(b=a+c).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.negation_display:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system and let } a,b \in P.\\
&a \not< b
\Longleftrightarrow
\forall c \in P\;(b \neq a+c).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.negation_formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system and let } a,b \in P.\\
&a \not< b
\Longleftrightarrow
\forall c \in P\;(b \neq a+c).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.failure_modes:
Strict inequality fails exactly when no additive witness in $P$ carries $a$ to
$b$. In that case, every nontrivial additive step from $a$ misses $b$.
nodes.failure_mode_decomposition:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system and let } a,b \in P.\\
&a \not< b
\Longleftrightarrow
\underbrace{\forall c \in P\;(b \neq a+c)}_{\text{every proposed additive witness fails}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.source_text:
The strict order records whether $b$ lies genuinely ahead of $a$ in the
counting structure. The witness $c$ is the amount of additive displacement
needed to move from $a$ to $b$.

\end{aligned}
\]

\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system and let } a,b \in P.\\

strictly below $b$, and $a$ is not equal to $b$. Thus $b$ neither lies ahead
of $a$ nor coincides with it.

$a$ to $b$. It is the additive order relation derived from the strict witness
definition.

Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For all $a,b,n \in P$,
\[
(a \cdot b)^n = a^n \cdot b^n.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:

Raising a product to a power distributes over the factors. The proof is
induction on $n$, using commutativity and associativity of multiplication to
rearrange the interleaved factors at each successor step.

nodes.name: Powers with Common Exponent Preserve Strict Order
nodes.question: State the theorem: Powers with Common Exponent Preserve Strict Order.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $a,b,n \in P$,
\[
a<b
\Longleftrightarrow
a^n<b^n.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $a,b,n \in P$,
\[
a<b
\Longleftrightarrow
a^n<b^n.
\]
nodes.source_text:
A positive exponent does not collapse the strict order between bases. Since
the exponent is a natural number, exponentiation repeatedly multiplies by
positive factors and preserves the order information.

nodes.source_text:
Strict growth in the exponent occurs exactly when the base is beyond the
multiplicative identity. If the base is $1$, all powers are $1$; if the base
is larger than $1$, each successor step in the exponent multiplies by a factor
that strictly increases the value.

nodes.name: $n < 2^n$ for All $n $
nodes.question: State the theorem: $n < 2^n$ for All $n $.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $2 \coloneqq S(1)$. For every $n \in P$,
\[
n < 2^n.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $2 \coloneqq S(1)$. For every $n \in P$,
\[
n < 2^n.
\]
nodes.source_text:
The base case $1 < 2 = 2^1$ holds by definition of $2$ and the strict order.
For the inductive step, assume $n < 2^n$. Then $2^{S(n)} = 2^n \cdot 2$.
Since $2^n > n \ge 1$, we have $2^n \cdot 2 > n \cdot 2 = n + n > n + 1 = S(n)$,
where the last step uses that $n \ge 1$ so $n + n > n + 1$. Hence $S(n) < 2^{S(n)}$.
The inequality $n < 2^n$ is the threshold that distinguishes the growth regimes
and reappears in every comparison between polynomial and exponential bounds.

nodes.name: Well-Ordering Principle
nodes.question: State the theorem: Well-Ordering Principle.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. Every nonempty subset of $P$ has a least
element with respect to the order $\le$ on $P$.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. Every nonempty subset of $P$ has a least
element with respect to the order $\le$ on $P$.
nodes.failure_modes:
The well-ordering principle would fail if some nonempty subset of $P$ had no
least element. That means for every candidate minimum, a strictly smaller
element of the subset exists, producing an infinite strictly descending chain
in $P$. Induction rules this out.
nodes.source_text:
The well-ordering principle is the order-theoretic complement to induction.
Induction says one can build up: start at $1$ and keep stepping forward.
Well-ordering says one can always descend to a minimum: any nonempty set has
a floor. Proof strategies that use well-ordering typically assume a property
fails somewhere, form the set of failures, extract its minimum by
well-ordering, and derive a contradiction from the minimality of that element.
used_by_titles: Less Than or Equal on a Peano System

nodes.name: Induction and Well-Ordering Are Equivalent
nodes.question: State the theorem: Induction and Well-Ordering Are Equivalent.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system equipped with the order $\le$. The following
are equivalent:
- The induction principle: for every predicate $\varphi$ on $P$, if
 $\varphi(1)$ holds and the successor step holds, then $\varphi(n)$ holds
 for all $n \in P$.
- The well-ordering principle: every nonempty subset of $P$ has a least
 element with respect to $\le$.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system equipped with the order $\le$. The following
are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item The induction principle: for every predicate $\varphi$ on $P$, if
 $\varphi(1)$ holds and the successor step holds, then $\varphi(n)$ holds
 for all $n \in P$.
 \item The well-ordering principle: every nonempty subset of $P$ has a least
 element with respect to $\le$.
\end{enumerate}
nodes.source_text:
Induction proves well-ordering by contrapositive: if a nonempty set $A$ had
no least element, the set of non-members of $A$ would be inductive, forcing
$A = \varnothing$, a contradiction. Well-ordering proves induction by forming
the set of elements where $\varphi$ fails and, if nonempty, extracting a
least failure to derive a contradiction with the successor step.

nodes.name: The Fraction-Pair Relation Is an Equivalence Relation
nodes.question: State the theorem: The Fraction-Pair Relation Is an Equivalence Relation.
nodes.statement_display: The relation $\sim$ is an equivalence relation on $W$.
nodes.statement_tex: The relation $\sim$ is an equivalence relation on $W$.
nodes.proof_sketch:
Step 1. Verify reflexivity.

Let $(a,b)\in W$. Since $W=\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\})$,
we have $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $b\neq 0$. To prove reflexivity, it is
necessary to show
\[
(a,b)\sim(a,b).
\]
By the definition of $\sim$, this is equivalent to showing
\[
ab=ba.
\]
This equality holds by commutativity of multiplication in $\mathbb{Z}$.
Therefore
\[
(a,b)\sim(a,b).
\]
Hence $\sim$ is reflexive.
Step 2. Verify symmetry.

Let $(a,b),(c,d)\in W$, and assume
\[
(a,b)\sim(c,d).
\]
By the definition of $\sim$, this means
\[
ad=bc.
\]
To prove symmetry, it is necessary to show
\[
(c,d)\sim(a,b).
\]
By the definition of $\sim$, this is equivalent to showing
\[
cb=da.
\]
From $ad=bc$, symmetry of equality gives
\[
bc=ad.
\]
By commutativity of multiplication in $\mathbb{Z}$,
\[
cb=bc
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
ad=da.
\]
Therefore
\[
cb=da.
\]
Hence
\[
(c,d)\sim(a,b).
\]
Thus $\sim$ is symmetric.
Step 3. Verify transitivity.

Let $(a,b),(c,d),(e,f)\in W$, and assume
\[
(a,b)\sim(c,d)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
(c,d)\sim(e,f).
\]
By the definition of $\sim$, these assumptions give
\[
ad=bc
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
cf=de.
\]
To prove transitivity, it is necessary to show
\[
(a,b)\sim(e,f),
\]
which means
\[
af=be.
\]

Multiplying the equality $ad=bc$ by $f$ gives
\[
adf=bcf.
\]
Multiplying the equality $cf=de$ by $b$ gives
\[
bcf=bde.
\]
Combining these two equalities gives
\[
adf=bde.
\]
Using associativity and commutativity of multiplication in $\mathbb{Z}$,
this may be rewritten as
\[
d(af)=d(be).
\]
Since $(c,d)\in W$, the second coordinate $d$ is nonzero. Therefore
cancellation by the nonzero integer $d$ gives
\[
af=be.
\]
Hence
\[
(a,b)\sim(e,f).
\]
Thus $\sim$ is transitive.
Step 4. Conclude that the relation is an equivalence relation.

The relation $\sim$ has been shown to be reflexive, symmetric, and
transitive. Therefore $\sim$ is an equivalence relation on $W$.
proof_steps:
Step 1. Verify reflexivity.

Let $(a,b)\in W$. Since $W=\mathbb{Z}\times(\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\})$,
we have $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $b\neq 0$. To prove reflexivity, it is

\[

\]
By the definition of $\sim$, this is equivalent to showing
\[
ab=ba.
\]
This equality holds by commutativity of multiplication in $\mathbb{Z}$.
Therefore
\[
(a,b)\sim(a,b).
\]
Hence $\sim$ is reflexive.

Step 2. Verify symmetry.

Let $(a,b),(c,d)\in W$, and assume
\[
(a,b)\sim(c,d).
\]
By the definition of $\sim$, this means
\[
ad=bc.
\]
To prove symmetry, it is necessary to show
\[
(c,d)\sim(a,b).
\]
By the definition of $\sim$, this is equivalent to showing
\[
cb=da.
\]
From $ad=bc$, symmetry of equality gives
\[
bc=ad.
\]
By commutativity of multiplication in $\mathbb{Z}$,
\[
cb=bc
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
ad=da.
\]
Therefore
\[
cb=da.
\]
Hence
\[
(c,d)\sim(a,b).
\]
Thus $\sim$ is symmetric.

Step 3. Verify transitivity.

Let $(a,b),(c,d),(e,f)\in W$, and assume
\[
(a,b)\sim(c,d)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
(c,d)\sim(e,f).
\]
By the definition of $\sim$, these assumptions give
\[
ad=bc
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
cf=de.
\]
To prove transitivity, it is necessary to show
\[
(a,b)\sim(e,f),
\]
which means
\[
af=be.
\]

Multiplying the equality $ad=bc$ by $f$ gives
\[
adf=bcf.
\]
Multiplying the equality $cf=de$ by $b$ gives
\[
bcf=bde.
\]
Combining these two equalities gives
\[
adf=bde.
\]
Using associativity and commutativity of multiplication in $\mathbb{Z}$,
this may be rewritten as
\[
d(af)=d(be).
\]
Since $(c,d)\in W$, the second coordinate $d$ is nonzero. Therefore
cancellation by the nonzero integer $d$ gives
\[
af=be.
\]
Hence
\[
(a,b)\sim(e,f).
\]
Thus $\sim$ is transitive.

Step 4. Conclude that the relation is an equivalence relation.

The relation $\sim$ has been shown to be reflexive, symmetric, and
transitive. Therefore $\sim$ is an equivalence relation on $W$.
nodes.proof_idea:
The proof is direct. Reflexivity follows from commutativity of integer
multiplication. Symmetry follows by reversing the equality and commuting
the products. Transitivity is the only substantive step: two cross-product
equalities are multiplied by the remaining denominators, combined, and
then cancellation by a nonzero integer produces the required cross-product
equality.

nodes.name: Positive cone
nodes.question: State the definition: Positive cone.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $F$ be a field. A subset $P\subset F$ is called a \emph{positive
cone} if it satisfies:
- if $a,b\in P$, then $a+b\in P$;
- if $a,b\in P$, then $ab\in P$;
- for every $a\in F$, exactly one of the following holds:
 \[
 a\in P,
 \qquad
 a=0,
 \qquad
 -a\in P.
 \]
Define the order relation by
\[
a<b \iff b-a\in P.
\]

nodes.question: State the definition: Densely ordered system.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $S$ be a set with a relation $<$. We say that $(S,<)$ is
\emph{densely ordered} if:
- $(S,<)$ is a simply ordered system; and
- for every $x,y\in S$ with $x<y$, there exists $z\in S$ such that
 \[
 x<z<y.

nodes.statement_tex:
Let $S$ be a set with a relation $<$. We say that $(S,<)$ is
\emph{densely ordered} if:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item $(S,<)$ is a simply ordered system; and
 \item for every $x,y\in S$ with $x<y$, there exists $z\in S$ such that
 \[
 x<z<y.
 \]
\end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Integral domain
nodes.question: State the definition: Integral domain.
nodes.statement_display:
A system
\[
(F,+,\cdot,0,1)
\]
is called an \emph{integral domain} if:
- $(F,+,0)$ is a commutative group;
- multiplication on $F$ is associative and commutative;
- $1\neq 0$ and
 \[
 \forall a\in F,\qquad 1\cdot a=a=a\cdot 1;
 \]
- multiplication distributes over addition;
- $F$ has no zero divisors, that is,
 \[
 \forall a,b\in F,\qquad ab=0 \Longrightarrow a=0 \text{ or } b=0.
 \]

nodes.question: State the definition: Field.
nodes.statement_display:
A system
\[
(F,+,\cdot,0,1)
\]
is called a \emph{field} if it is an integral domain and satisfies:
\[
\forall a,b\in F,\qquad b\neq 0 \Longrightarrow \exists x\in F\;(b\cdot x=a).

Equivalently, every nonzero element of $F$ has a multiplicative inverse.

nodes.name: $ $ Is an Integral Domain
nodes.question: State the theorem: $ $ Is an Integral Domain.
nodes.statement_display:
With the operations of
\hyperref[def:rational-operations]{Definition~\ref*{def:rational-operations}},
the system
\[
(\mathbb{Q},+,\cdot,0,1)
\]
is an integral domain.
nodes.statement_tex:
With the operations of
\hyperref[def:rational-operations]{Definition~\ref*{def:rational-operations}},
the system
\[
(\mathbb{Q},+,\cdot,0,1)
\]
is an integral domain.
nodes.proof_sketch:
\textbf{Professional Standard Proof.}~\\
We verify the five conditions of the integral domain definition.

\textbf{(1) $(\mathbb{Q},+,0)$ is a commutative group.}

\emph{Closure.} If $[(a,b)],[(c,d)]\in\mathbb{Q}$ then
$[(ad+bc,bd)]\in\mathbb{Q}$ since $bd\neq 0$.

\emph{Associativity.} Let $p = [(a,b)]$, $q = [(c,d)]$, $r = [(e,f)]$.
Then
\begin{align*}
(p+q)+r &= [(ad+bc,bd)] + [(e,f)] = [((ad+bc)f + bd\cdot e,\; bdf)], \\
p+(q+r) &= [(a,b)] + [(cf+de,df)] = [(a\cdot df + b(cf+de),\; bdf)].
\end{align*}
The numerators are $(adf + bcf + bde)$ in both cases, so the sums are equal.

\emph{Identity.} $[(a,b)] + [(0,1)] = [(a\cdot 1 + b\cdot 0, b\cdot 1)] = [(a,b)]$.

\emph{Inverses.} $[(a,b)] + [(-a,b)] = [(ab - ab, b^2)] = [(0,b^2)] = 0$,
since $(0,b^2)\sim(0,1)$.

\emph{Commutativity.} $[(a,b)]+[(c,d)] = [(ad+bc,bd)] = [(cb+da,db)] = [(c,d)]+[(a,b)]$.

\textbf{(2) Multiplication is associative and commutative.}

\emph{Associativity.}
$([(a,b)]\cdot[(c,d)])\cdot[(e,f)] = [(ac,bd)]\cdot[(e,f)] = [(ace,bdf)]$.
$[(a,b)]\cdot([(c,d)]\cdot[(e,f)]) = [(a,b)]\cdot[(ce,df)] = [(ace,bdf)]$.

\emph{Commutativity.}
$[(a,b)]\cdot[(c,d)] = [(ac,bd)] = [(ca,db)] = [(c,d)]\cdot[(a,b)]$.

\textbf{(3) $1\neq 0$ and $1$ is the multiplicative identity.}

$[(1,1)]\neq[(0,1)]$ since $1\cdot 1 = 1\neq 0 = 0\cdot 1$.
$[(1,1)]\cdot[(a,b)] = [(1\cdot a, 1\cdot b)] = [(a,b)]$.

\textbf{(4) Multiplication distributes over addition.}

\begin{align*}
[(a,b)]\cdot([(c,d)]+[(e,f)])
&= [(a,b)]\cdot[(cf+de,df)] \\
&= [(a(cf+de),\; b\cdot df)] \\
&= [(acf+ade,\; bdf)].
\end{align*}
\begin{align*}
[(a,b)]\cdot[(c,d)] + [(a,b)]\cdot[(e,f)]
&= [(ac,bd)] + [(ae,bf)] \\
&= [(ac\cdot bf + bd\cdot ae,\; bd\cdot bf)] \\
&= [(abcf + abde,\; b^2df)].
\end{align*}
These two classes are equal iff $(acf+ade)(b^2df) = (abcf+abde)(bdf)$,
which simplifies to $ab^2df(cf+de) = ab(bdf)(cf+de)$, i.e.\ $b^2df = b^2df$.
True.

\textbf{(5) $\mathbb{Q}$ has no zero divisors.}

Suppose $[(a,b)]\cdot[(c,d)] = 0$. Then $[(ac,bd)] = [(0,1)]$, so
$(ac,bd)\sim(0,1)$, meaning $ac\cdot 1 = bd\cdot 0 = 0$. Thus $ac = 0$.
Since $\mathbb{Z}$ is an integral domain, $a=0$ or $c=0$. By the zero class
criterion, $a=0$ iff $[(a,b)] = 0$ and $c=0$ iff $[(c,d)] = 0$.
Therefore $[(a,b)]=0$ or $[(c,d)]=0$.

Since all five conditions hold, $(\mathbb{Q},+,\cdot,0,1)$ is an integral domain.
nodes.proof_idea:
The proof is a systematic verification of each axiom. The substantive
content lies in three places: the associativity of addition (which requires
expanding both sides and comparing numerators), the distributivity check
(which reduces to a cross-multiplication equality), and the no-zero-divisors
property (which reduces $\mathbb{Q}$-level zeroes to the corresponding fact
in $\mathbb{Z}$, which is an integral domain by construction).

All other axioms are direct computations from the operation definitions and
the arithmetic of $\mathbb{Z}$.

nodes.name: $ $ Is a Field
nodes.question: State the theorem: $ $ Is a Field.
nodes.statement_display:
With the operations of
\hyperref[def:rational-operations]{Definition~\ref*{def:rational-operations}},
the system
\[
(\mathbb{Q},+,\cdot,0,1)
\]
is a field.
nodes.statement_tex:
With the operations of
\hyperref[def:rational-operations]{Definition~\ref*{def:rational-operations}},
the system
\[
(\mathbb{Q},+,\cdot,0,1)
\]
is a field.
nodes.proof_sketch:
Step 1. Recall what must be shown.

By the field definition, a field is an integral domain in which every
nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse. We have already established
that $\mathbb{Q}$ is an integral domain. It therefore suffices to show:
\[
\forall\, [(a,b)]\in\mathbb{Q},\quad [(a,b)]\neq 0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\exists\, y\in\mathbb{Q},\; [(a,b)]\cdot y = 1.
\]
Step 2. Let $[(a,b)]\in\mathbb{Q}$ be nonzero.

By the zero class criterion, $[(a,b)] = 0$ iff $a = 0$. Since we assumed
$[(a,b)]\neq 0$, we have $a\neq 0$.
Step 3. Propose the candidate inverse.

Define $y := [(b,a)]$. We must first check this is well-formed: since
$a\neq 0$ (established in Step 2) and $b\neq 0$ (since $(a,b)\in W$),
the pair $(b,a)\in W$, so $[(b,a)]\in\mathbb{Q}$.
Step 4. Verify that $[(a,b)]\cdot[(b,a)] = 1$.

By the multiplication formula:
\[
[(a,b)]\cdot[(b,a)]
= [(a\cdot b,\; b\cdot a)]
= [(ab,\; ab)].
\]
We check $(ab,ab)\sim(1,1)$: by the definition of $\sim$, this requires
$ab\cdot 1 = ab\cdot 1$, which is trivially true.

Also, $ab\neq 0$ since $a\neq 0$ and $b\neq 0$ and $\mathbb{Z}$ has no
zero divisors. So $(ab,ab)\in W$ and the class $[(ab,ab)]$ is well-formed.

Since $(ab,ab)\sim(1,1)$, we have $[(ab,ab)] = [(1,1)] = 1$.

Therefore:
\[
[(a,b)]\cdot[(b,a)] = 1.
\]
Step 5. Conclude.

We have exhibited an element $y = [(b,a)]\in\mathbb{Q}$ such that
$[(a,b)]\cdot y = 1$. Since $[(a,b)]$ was an arbitrary nonzero element
of $\mathbb{Q}$, every nonzero element of $\mathbb{Q}$ has a multiplicative
inverse.

Combined with the integral domain theorem, $(\mathbb{Q},+,\cdot,0,1)$ is
a field.

The proof has a single substantive step: showing that for a nonzero

The key computation is that $[(ab,ab)] = 1$, which follows from the

well-formedness of the fraction-pair).

The proof builds on the integral domain theorem, which carries all of the
axiom-checking work. The field proof adds only one condition to that package.

nodes.name: Negative Exponents Agree with Inverse Powers
nodes.question: State the theorem: Negative Exponents Agree with Inverse Powers.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $F$ be a field, let $x\in F$ with $x\neq 0$, and let $m,n\in\mathbb{Z}$.
Then
\[
x^{-m}=(x^{-1})^m=(x^m)^{-1}.
\]
Moreover, the usual laws of exponents continue to hold for integer exponents.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $F$ be a field, let $x\in F$ with $x\neq 0$, and let $m,n\in\mathbb{Z}$.
Then
\[
x^{-m}=(x^{-1})^m=(x^m)^{-1}.
\]
Moreover, the usual laws of exponents continue to hold for integer exponents.
nodes.proof_sketch:
Step B1. Expand $x^{k+1}$ using the recursive definition.

By \hyperref[def:nonneg-integer-exponents-field]{Definition~\ref*{def:nonneg-integer-exponents-field}},
\[
x^{k+1} = x^k \cdot x.
\]
Step B2. Invert the product.

By the field theorem on the inverse of a product (the inverse reverses order:
$(a\cdot b)^{-1} = b^{-1}\cdot a^{-1}$, which equals $a^{-1}\cdot b^{-1}$
by commutativity of multiplication),
\[
(x^{k+1})^{-1} = (x^k\cdot x)^{-1} = x^{-1}\cdot (x^k)^{-1}.
\]
Step B3. Apply the inductive hypothesis.

By the inductive hypothesis, $(x^k)^{-1} = (x^{-1})^k$.  Substituting:
\[
x^{-1}\cdot(x^k)^{-1} = x^{-1}\cdot(x^{-1})^k.
\]
Step B4. Collapse using the recursive definition applied to $x^{-1}$.

By \hyperref[def:nonneg-integer-exponents-field]{Definition~\ref*{def:nonneg-integer-exponents-field}}
applied to the base element $x^{-1}$:
\[
(x^{-1})^{k+1} = (x^{-1})^k \cdot x^{-1} = x^{-1}\cdot(x^{-1})^k.
\]
(using commutativity of multiplication for the last step).  Therefore:
\[
(x^{k+1})^{-1} = (x^{-1})^{k+1}.
\]
Step B5. Close the induction.

By the principle of mathematical induction, $(x^m)^{-1} = (x^{-1})^m$ for
all $m\in\mathbb{N}$.  Combined with Part A:
\[
x^{-m} = (x^{-1})^m = (x^m)^{-1}. \qedhere
\]
proof_steps:
Step B1. Expand $x^{k+1}$ using the recursive definition.

By \hyperref[def:nonneg-integer-exponents-field]{Definition~\ref*{def:nonneg-integer-exponents-field}},
\[
x^{k+1} = x^k \cdot x.
\]

Step B2. Invert the product.

By the field theorem on the inverse of a product (the inverse reverses order:
$(a\cdot b)^{-1} = b^{-1}\cdot a^{-1}$, which equals $a^{-1}\cdot b^{-1}$
by commutativity of multiplication),
\[
(x^{k+1})^{-1} = (x^k\cdot x)^{-1} = x^{-1}\cdot (x^k)^{-1}.
\]

Step B3. Apply the inductive hypothesis.

By the inductive hypothesis, $(x^k)^{-1} = (x^{-1})^k$.  Substituting:
\[
x^{-1}\cdot(x^k)^{-1} = x^{-1}\cdot(x^{-1})^k.
\]

Step B4. Collapse using the recursive definition applied to $x^{-1}$.

By \hyperref[def:nonneg-integer-exponents-field]{Definition~\ref*{def:nonneg-integer-exponents-field}}
applied to the base element $x^{-1}$:
\[
(x^{-1})^{k+1} = (x^{-1})^k \cdot x^{-1} = x^{-1}\cdot(x^{-1})^k.
\]
(using commutativity of multiplication for the last step).  Therefore:
\[
(x^{k+1})^{-1} = (x^{-1})^{k+1}.
\]

Step B5. Close the induction.

By the principle of mathematical induction, $(x^m)^{-1} = (x^{-1})^m$ for
all $m\in\mathbb{N}$.  Combined with Part A:
\[
x^{-m} = (x^{-1})^m = (x^m)^{-1}. \qedhere
\]
nodes.proof_idea:
The first equality is definitional.  The second requires induction because
it asks about the relationship between two independently defined operations:
natural-number exponentiation $x^m$ (built by repeated multiplication) and
the field inverse $(-)^{-1}$ (an axiomatically given operation).  The inductive
step turns on the product-inversion identity $(ab)^{-1} = b^{-1}a^{-1}$, which
lets the inversion distribute through one factor at a time, consuming $x^k$
via the inductive hypothesis.  The base case $m=0$ requires
\hyperref[thm:one-inverse-is-one]{Theorem~\ref*{thm:one-inverse-is-one}} to
identify $1^{-1} = 1$.

nodes.name: Power of a Product in a Field
nodes.question: State the theorem: Power of a Product in a Field.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(F,+,\cdot,0,1)$ be a field. Let $q,r\in F\setminus\{0\}$ and let
$a\in\mathbb{Z}$. Then
\[
(qr)^a=q^a r^a.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(F,+,\cdot,0,1)$ be a field. Let $q,r\in F\setminus\{0\}$ and let
$a\in\mathbb{Z}$. Then
\[
(qr)^a=q^a r^a.
\]
nodes.proof_sketch:
Step 1. Prove the nonnegative exponent case.

Assume first that $a\ge 0$. Then $a\in\mathbb{N}$. For natural-number
powers, the product law for exponents gives
\[
(qr)^a=q^a r^a.
\]
This proves the result for all nonnegative integer exponents.
Step 2. Reduce the negative exponent case to a positive exponent.

Assume now that $a<0$. Then there exists $n\in\mathbb{N}$ with
$n>0$ such that
\[
a=-n.
\]
Since $q,r\in F\setminus\{0\}$, both $q$ and $r$ are nonzero. Because
$F$ is a field, the product of two nonzero elements is nonzero, so
\[
qr\neq 0.
\]
Therefore the negative power $(qr)^{-n}$ is defined.
Step 3. Expand the negative power of the product.

By the definition of negative integer exponents,
\[
(qr)^a=(qr)^{-n}=\frac{1}{(qr)^n}.
\]
Since $n\in\mathbb{N}$, the natural-number product law gives
\[
(qr)^n=q^n r^n.
\]
Substituting this into the previous equality gives
\[
(qr)^a=\frac{1}{q^n r^n}.
\]
Step 4. Split the inverse of the product.

Because $q\neq 0$ and $r\neq 0$, the powers $q^n$ and $r^n$ are
nonzero. Hence
\[
q^n r^n\neq 0.
\]
In a field, the inverse of a product of nonzero elements is the product
of the inverses. Thus
\[
\frac{1}{q^n r^n}=\frac{1}{q^n}\frac{1}{r^n}.
\]
Step 5. Convert the inverses back into negative powers.

By the definition of negative integer exponents,
\[
\frac{1}{q^n}=q^{-n}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\frac{1}{r^n}=r^{-n}.
\]
Therefore
\[
(qr)^a
=
\frac{1}{q^n r^n}
=
\frac{1}{q^n}\frac{1}{r^n}
=
q^{-n}r^{-n}.
\]
Since $a=-n$, this becomes
\[
(qr)^a=q^a r^a.
\]
This proves the theorem.

case is applied, and then the inverse of a product is split into the product
of inverses.

nodes.question: State the theorem: Integer Exponent Addition Law.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(F,+,\cdot,0,1)$ be a field, let $q\in F\setminus\{0\}$, and let
$a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$. Then
\[
q^a q^b=q^{a+b}.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(F,+,\cdot,0,1)$ be a field, let $q\in F\setminus\{0\}$, and let
$a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$. Then
\[
q^a q^b=q^{a+b}.
\]
nodes.proof_idea:
The proof is a case split on $\mathrm{sgn}(a)$ and $\mathrm{sgn}(b)$, giving
four main cases (Case 2 further splits into three sub-cases by comparing $a$
and $n = -b$).  The natural-number case is the inductive spine; every other
case reduces to it plus the identity $(q^n)^{-1} = q^{-n}$ and the
product-inversion identity $(uv)^{-1} = v^{-1}u^{-1}$.

The key insight in Case 2 is that $q^a\cdot(q^n)^{-1}$ requires cancelling
$q^{\min(a,n)}$ factors, leaving either a positive or negative residual power
depending on whether $a\geq n$ or $a < n$.  Case 4 is cleaner: two negative
exponents convert to two inverses, whose product inverts as a whole via the
product-inversion identity, and the natural-number law handles the sum of the
absolute values.
nodes.text_preview: [Integer Exponent Addition Law] Let $(F,+, ,0,1)$ be a field, let $q F \ 0\ $, and let $a,b $. Then \[ q^a q^b=q^ a+b . \]

nodes.name: Power of a Power in a Field
nodes.question: State the theorem: Power of a Power in a Field.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(F,+,\cdot,0,1)$ be a field, let $q\in F\setminus\{0\}$, and let
$a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$. Then
\[
(q^a)^b=q^{ab}.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(F,+,\cdot,0,1)$ be a field, let $q\in F\setminus\{0\}$, and let
$a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$. Then
\[
(q^a)^b=q^{ab}.
\]
nodes.proof_sketch:
\textbf{Professional Standard Proof.}~\\
We split according to the sign of $b$.

If $b=0$, then
\[
(q^a)^0=1=q^0=q^{a\cdot 0}.
\]

If $b=n>0$, we argue by induction on $n$.  For $n=1$ the identity is
\[
(q^a)^1=q^a=q^{a\cdot 1}.
\]
Assume $(q^a)^n=q^{an}$.  Then
\[
(q^a)^{n+1}=(q^a)^n q^a=q^{an}q^a=q^{an+a}=q^{a(n+1)},
\]
using the induction hypothesis and the integer exponent addition law.

Finally, let $b=-n$ with $n>0$.  Then
\[
(q^a)^b=(q^a)^{-n}=((q^a)^{-1})^n=(q^{-a})^n=q^{(-a)n}=q^{a(-n)}=q^{ab},
\]
using the theorem on negative exponents and the already established
positive-exponent case.
nodes.proof_idea:
The proof separates the positive, zero, and negative cases for the outer
exponent $b$.  The positive case is an induction on $b$, with the induction
step supplied by the exponent addition law.  The negative case rewrites the
outer negative exponent as a positive power of an inverse and then applies
the positive case to $q^{-a}$.  This reduces the entire statement to the two
basic mechanisms already built into the integer exponent calculus: recursion
for positive powers and inversion for negative powers.

nodes.name: Zero product
nodes.question: State the theorem: Zero product.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $F$ be a field and let $a\in F$. Then
\[
a\cdot 0 = 0.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $F$ be a field and let $a\in F$. Then
\[
a\cdot 0 = 0.
\]
nodes.proof_sketch:
Step 1. Use the additive identity law to write $0$ as $0 + 0$.

By the field axiom for the additive identity,
\[
0 + 0 = 0.
\]
Step 2. Multiply both sides on the left by $a$.

\[
a \cdot 0 = a \cdot (0 + 0).
\]
Step 3. Apply distributivity.

By the distributivity axiom,
\[
a \cdot (0 + 0) = a\cdot 0 + a\cdot 0.
\]
Combining Steps 2 and 3:
\[
a\cdot 0 = a\cdot 0 + a\cdot 0.
\]
Step 4. Add the additive inverse of $a\cdot 0$ to both sides.

Adding $-(a\cdot 0)$ to both sides of $a\cdot 0 = a\cdot 0 + a\cdot 0$:
\[
a\cdot 0 + (-(a\cdot 0)) = a\cdot 0 + a\cdot 0 + (-(a\cdot 0)).
\]
Step 5. Apply the additive inverse axiom and associativity.

The left-hand side is $0$ by the additive inverse axiom.  On the right,
associativity of addition gives
\[
a\cdot 0 + (a\cdot 0 + (-(a\cdot 0))) = a\cdot 0 + 0 = a\cdot 0.
\]
Therefore
\[
0 = a\cdot 0.
\]
Step 6. Conclude.

By commutativity of equality, $a\cdot 0 = 0$.
proof_steps:
Step 1. Use the additive identity law to write $0$ as $0 + 0$.

By the field axiom for the additive identity,
\[
0 + 0 = 0.
\]

Step 2. Multiply both sides on the left by $a$.

\[
a \cdot 0 = a \cdot (0 + 0).
\]

Step 3. Apply distributivity.

By the distributivity axiom,
\[
a \cdot (0 + 0) = a\cdot 0 + a\cdot 0.
\]
Combining Steps 2 and 3:
\[
a\cdot 0 = a\cdot 0 + a\cdot 0.
\]

Step 4. Add the additive inverse of $a\cdot 0$ to both sides.

Adding $-(a\cdot 0)$ to both sides of $a\cdot 0 = a\cdot 0 + a\cdot 0$:
\[
a\cdot 0 + (-(a\cdot 0)) = a\cdot 0 + a\cdot 0 + (-(a\cdot 0)).
\]

Step 5. Apply the additive inverse axiom and associativity.

The left-hand side is $0$ by the additive inverse axiom.  On the right,
associativity of addition gives
\[
a\cdot 0 + (a\cdot 0 + (-(a\cdot 0))) = a\cdot 0 + 0 = a\cdot 0.
\]
Therefore
\[
0 = a\cdot 0.
\]

Step 6. Conclude.

By commutativity of equality, $a\cdot 0 = 0$.
nodes.proof_idea:
The key move is writing $0 = 0 + 0$ using the additive identity law, then
distributing $a$ across the sum to obtain $a\cdot 0 = a\cdot 0 + a\cdot 0$.
This says $a\cdot 0$ is a solution to $x = x + a\cdot 0$, and the only
solution to that equation is $x = 0$.  Cancellation is performed directly
by adding the additive inverse rather than invoking the cancellation theorem,
keeping the proof self-contained within the field axioms alone.

nodes.name: Double negation
nodes.question: State the theorem: Double negation.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $F$ be a field and let $a\in F$. Then
\[
-(-a) = a.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $F$ be a field and let $a\in F$. Then
\[
-(-a) = a.
\]
nodes.proof_sketch:
Step 1. Observe that $a$ is an additive inverse of $-a$.

By the additive inverse axiom applied to $a$,
\[
a + (-a) = 0.
\]
By commutativity of addition,
\[
(-a) + a = 0.
\]
So $a$ satisfies the defining condition for the additive inverse of $-a$.
Step 2. Observe that $-(-a)$ is also an additive inverse of $-a$.

By the additive inverse axiom applied to $-a$,
\[
(-a) + (-(-a)) = 0.
\]
So $-(-a)$ also satisfies the defining condition for the additive inverse of $-a$.
Step 3. Show additive inverses are unique via cancellation.

From Steps 1 and 2:
\[
(-a) + a = 0 = (-a) + (-(-a)).
\]
By additive cancellation (with $b := a$, $c := -(-a)$, and the common
left summand $-a$), we conclude
\[
a = -(-a).
\]
Step 4. Conclude.

By symmetry of equality, $-(-a) = a$.
proof_steps:
Step 1. Observe that $a$ is an additive inverse of $-a$.

By the additive inverse axiom applied to $a$,
\[
a + (-a) = 0.
\]
By commutativity of addition,
\[
(-a) + a = 0.
\]
So $a$ satisfies the defining condition for the additive inverse of $-a$.

Step 2. Observe that $-(-a)$ is also an additive inverse of $-a$.

By the additive inverse axiom applied to $-a$,
\[
(-a) + (-(-a)) = 0.
\]
So $-(-a)$ also satisfies the defining condition for the additive inverse of $-a$.

Step 3. Show additive inverses are unique via cancellation.

From Steps 1 and 2:
\[
(-a) + a = 0 = (-a) + (-(-a)).
\]
By additive cancellation (with $b := a$, $c := -(-a)$, and the common
left summand $-a$), we conclude
\[
a = -(-a).
\]

Step 4. Conclude.

By symmetry of equality, $-(-a) = a$.
nodes.proof_idea:
Both $a$ and $-(-a)$ satisfy the defining equation for the additive inverse
of $-a$, namely $(-a) + x = 0$.  Since additive cancellation forces any two
solutions to that equation to be equal, they must coincide.  This is the
standard uniqueness-of-inverses argument: exhibit two objects satisfying the
same defining property, then cancel to conclude they are equal.
nodes.text_preview: [Double negation] Let $F$ be a field and let $a F$. Then \[ -(-a) = a. \]

nodes.name: Negation of a product
nodes.question: State the theorem: Negation of a product.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $F$ be a field and let $a,b\in F$. Then
\[
-(a\cdot b) = (-a)\cdot b = a\cdot(-b).
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $F$ be a field and let $a,b\in F$. Then
\[
-(a\cdot b) = (-a)\cdot b = a\cdot(-b).
\]
nodes.proof_sketch:
Step A1. Compute $a\cdot b + (-a)\cdot b$.

By distributivity (right),
\[
a\cdot b + (-a)\cdot b = (a + (-a))\cdot b.
\]
Step A2. Apply the additive inverse axiom.

By the additive inverse axiom, $a + (-a) = 0$.  Therefore,
\[
(a + (-a))\cdot b = 0\cdot b.
\]
Step A3. Apply the zero product theorem.

By \hyperref[thm:zero-product]{Theorem~\ref*{thm:zero-product}} (with the
roles of $a$ and $b$ swapped, using commutativity of multiplication),
$0\cdot b = 0$.  Therefore,
\[
a\cdot b + (-a)\cdot b = 0.
\]
Step A4. Conclude by uniqueness of additive inverses.

The equation $a\cdot b + (-a)\cdot b = 0$ states that $(-a)\cdot b$ is an
additive inverse of $a\cdot b$.  By additive cancellation, additive inverses
are unique.  Therefore,
\[
(-a)\cdot b = -(a\cdot b).
\]

\textbf{Part B: $a\cdot(-b) = -(a\cdot b)$.}
Step B1. Compute $a\cdot b + a\cdot(-b)$.

By distributivity (left),
\[
a\cdot b + a\cdot(-b) = a\cdot(b + (-b)).
\]
Step B2. Apply the additive inverse axiom.

By the additive inverse axiom, $b + (-b) = 0$.  Therefore,
\[
a\cdot(b + (-b)) = a\cdot 0.
\]
Step B3. Apply the zero product theorem.

By \hyperref[thm:zero-product]{Theorem~\ref*{thm:zero-product}},
$a\cdot 0 = 0$.  Therefore,
\[
a\cdot b + a\cdot(-b) = 0.
\]
Step B4. Conclude by uniqueness of additive inverses.

The equation $a\cdot b + a\cdot(-b) = 0$ states that $a\cdot(-b)$ is an
additive inverse of $a\cdot b$.  By additive cancellation, additive inverses
are unique.  Therefore,
\[
a\cdot(-b) = -(a\cdot b).
\]

\textbf{Conclusion.}

Combining Parts A and B:
\[
-(a\cdot b) = (-a)\cdot b = a\cdot(-b). \qedhere
\]
proof_steps:
Step A1. Compute $a\cdot b + (-a)\cdot b$.

By distributivity (right),
\[
a\cdot b + (-a)\cdot b = (a + (-a))\cdot b.
\]

Step A2. Apply the additive inverse axiom.

By the additive inverse axiom, $a + (-a) = 0$.  Therefore,
\[
(a + (-a))\cdot b = 0\cdot b.
\]

Step A3. Apply the zero product theorem.

By \hyperref[thm:zero-product]{Theorem~\ref*{thm:zero-product}} (with the
roles of $a$ and $b$ swapped, using commutativity of multiplication),
$0\cdot b = 0$.  Therefore,
\[
a\cdot b + (-a)\cdot b = 0.
\]

Step A4. Conclude by uniqueness of additive inverses.

The equation $a\cdot b + (-a)\cdot b = 0$ states that $(-a)\cdot b$ is an
additive inverse of $a\cdot b$.  By additive cancellation, additive inverses
are unique.  Therefore,
\[
(-a)\cdot b = -(a\cdot b).
\]

\textbf{Part B: $a\cdot(-b) = -(a\cdot b)$.}

Step B1. Compute $a\cdot b + a\cdot(-b)$.

By distributivity (left),
\[
a\cdot b + a\cdot(-b) = a\cdot(b + (-b)).
\]

Step B2. Apply the additive inverse axiom.

By the additive inverse axiom, $b + (-b) = 0$.  Therefore,
\[
a\cdot(b + (-b)) = a\cdot 0.
\]

Step B3. Apply the zero product theorem.

By \hyperref[thm:zero-product]{Theorem~\ref*{thm:zero-product}},
$a\cdot 0 = 0$.  Therefore,
\[
a\cdot b + a\cdot(-b) = 0.
\]

Step B4. Conclude by uniqueness of additive inverses.

The equation $a\cdot b + a\cdot(-b) = 0$ states that $a\cdot(-b)$ is an
additive inverse of $a\cdot b$.  By additive cancellation, additive inverses
are unique.  Therefore,
\[
a\cdot(-b) = -(a\cdot b).
\]

\textbf{Conclusion.}

Combining Parts A and B:
\[
-(a\cdot b) = (-a)\cdot b = a\cdot(-b). \qedhere
\]
nodes.proof_idea:
Both identities use the same strategy: show that the candidate equals
$-(a\cdot b)$ by verifying it sums with $a\cdot b$ to give $0$, then invoke
uniqueness of additive inverses via cancellation.  The computation in each
case is one application of distributivity, one application of the additive
inverse axiom, and one application of the zero product theorem.  Part A uses
right-distributivity; Part B uses left-distributivity.

nodes.name: Product of negatives
nodes.question: State the corollary: Product of negatives.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $F$ be a field and let $a,b\in F$. Then
\[
(-a)\cdot(-b) = a\cdot b.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $F$ be a field and let $a,b\in F$. Then
\[
(-a)\cdot(-b) = a\cdot b.
\]
nodes.proof_sketch:
Step 1. Apply the negation of a product theorem to the outer negation.

By \hyperref[thm:negation-of-product]{Theorem~\ref*{thm:negation-of-product}}
with $a$ replaced by $a$ and $b$ replaced by $-b$:
\[
(-a)\cdot(-b) = -(a\cdot(-b)).
\]
Step 2. Apply the negation of a product theorem to the inner term.

By \hyperref[thm:negation-of-product]{Theorem~\ref*{thm:negation-of-product}},
\[
a\cdot(-b) = -(a\cdot b).
\]
Substituting into Step 1:
\[
(-a)\cdot(-b) = -(-(a\cdot b)).
\]
Step 3. Apply double negation.

By \hyperref[thm:double-negation]{Theorem~\ref*{thm:double-negation}},
\[
-(-(a\cdot b)) = a\cdot b.
\]
Step 4. Conclude.

Chaining Steps 1--3:
\[
(-a)\cdot(-b) = -(-(a\cdot b)) = a\cdot b. \qedhere
\]
proof_steps:
Step 1. Apply the negation of a product theorem to the outer negation.

By \hyperref[thm:negation-of-product]{Theorem~\ref*{thm:negation-of-product}}
with $a$ replaced by $a$ and $b$ replaced by $-b$:
\[
(-a)\cdot(-b) = -(a\cdot(-b)).
\]

Step 2. Apply the negation of a product theorem to the inner term.

By \hyperref[thm:negation-of-product]{Theorem~\ref*{thm:negation-of-product}},
\[
a\cdot(-b) = -(a\cdot b).
\]
Substituting into Step 1:
\[
(-a)\cdot(-b) = -(-(a\cdot b)).
\]

Step 3. Apply double negation.

By \hyperref[thm:double-negation]{Theorem~\ref*{thm:double-negation}},
\[
-(-(a\cdot b)) = a\cdot b.
\]

Step 4. Conclude.

Chaining Steps 1--3:
\[
(-a)\cdot(-b) = -(-(a\cdot b)) = a\cdot b. \qedhere
\]
nodes.proof_idea:
This corollary is a two-line chain from the negation of a product theorem
and double negation.  The negation of a product theorem is applied twice in
sequence: first to pull $(-a)$ out of the product, producing $-(a\cdot(-b))$,
then to pull $(-b)$ out, producing $-(-(a\cdot b))$.  Double negation then
collapses the two negation signs to nothing.  No field axioms are cited
directly; all work was done in the two preceding theorems.

nodes.name: Additive cancellation
nodes.question: State the theorem: Additive cancellation.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $F$ be a field and let $a,b,c\in F$. If
\[
a + c = b + c,
\]
then $a = b$.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $F$ be a field and let $a,b,c\in F$. If
\[
a + c = b + c,
\]
then $a = b$.
nodes.proof_sketch:
Step 1. State the hypothesis.

Assume $a + c = b + c$.
Step 2. Add $-c$ to both sides.

Since $-c\in F$ (additive inverses exist in $F$), add $-c$ to both sides:
\[
(a + c) + (-c) = (b + c) + (-c).
\]
Step 3. Apply associativity of addition to both sides.

By associativity,
\[
(a + c) + (-c) = a + (c + (-c))
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
(b + c) + (-c) = b + (c + (-c)).
\]
Step 4. Apply the additive inverse axiom.

By the additive inverse axiom, $c + (-c) = 0$.  Therefore:
\[
a + (c + (-c)) = a + 0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
b + (c + (-c)) = b + 0.
\]
Step 5. Apply the additive identity axiom.

By the additive identity axiom, $a + 0 = a$ and $b + 0 = b$.
Step 6. Conclude.

Chaining Steps 2--5:
\[
a = a + 0 = a + (c + (-c)) = (a+c) + (-c) = (b+c) + (-c) = b + (c+(-c)) = b + 0 = b.
\]
Therefore $a = b$.
proof_steps:
Step 1. State the hypothesis.

Assume $a + c = b + c$.

Step 2. Add $-c$ to both sides.

Since $-c\in F$ (additive inverses exist in $F$), add $-c$ to both sides:
\[
(a + c) + (-c) = (b + c) + (-c).
\]

Step 3. Apply associativity of addition to both sides.

By associativity,
\[
(a + c) + (-c) = a + (c + (-c))
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
(b + c) + (-c) = b + (c + (-c)).
\]

Step 4. Apply the additive inverse axiom.

By the additive inverse axiom, $c + (-c) = 0$.  Therefore:
\[
a + (c + (-c)) = a + 0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
b + (c + (-c)) = b + 0.
\]

Step 5. Apply the additive identity axiom.

By the additive identity axiom, $a + 0 = a$ and $b + 0 = b$.

Step 6. Conclude.

Chaining Steps 2--5:
\[
a = a + 0 = a + (c + (-c)) = (a+c) + (-c) = (b+c) + (-c) = b + (c+(-c)) = b + 0 = b.
\]
Therefore $a = b$.
nodes.proof_idea:
The proof adds the additive inverse $-c$ to both sides of the hypothesis,
then unwinds the result using associativity, the additive inverse axiom, and
the additive identity axiom.  Each step cites exactly one field axiom.  The
conclusion $a = b$ is reached by a chain of equalities with no auxiliary
lemmas required.
nodes.text_preview: [Additive cancellation] Let $F$ be a field and let $a,b,c F$. If \[ a + c = b + c, \] then $a = b$.

nodes.name: Multiplicative cancellation
nodes.question: State the theorem: Multiplicative cancellation.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $F$ be a field and let $a,b,c\in F$ with $c\neq 0$. If
\[
a\cdot c = b\cdot c,
\]
then $a = b$.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $F$ be a field and let $a,b,c\in F$ with $c\neq 0$. If
\[
a\cdot c = b\cdot c,
\]
then $a = b$.
nodes.proof_sketch:
\textbf{Professional Standard Proof.}~\\
Assume $a\cdot c=b\cdot c$ with $c\neq 0$.  Since $F$ is a field, $c$ has a
multiplicative inverse $c^{-1}$.  Multiply the given equality on the right by
$c^{-1}$:
\[
(a\cdot c)\cdot c^{-1}=(b\cdot c)\cdot c^{-1}.
\]
By associativity,
\[
a\cdot(c\cdot c^{-1})=b\cdot(c\cdot c^{-1}).
\]
Since $c\cdot c^{-1}=1$, this becomes
\[
a\cdot 1=b\cdot 1.
\]
By the multiplicative identity axiom, $a=b$.
nodes.proof_idea:
The proof multiplies both sides of the equation by the inverse of the common
nonzero factor.  Associativity moves the factor $c^{-1}$ next to $c$, the
inverse axiom collapses $c\cdot c^{-1}$ to $1$, and the identity axiom then
removes the surviving factor of $1$.  This is the multiplicative analogue of
the usual additive cancellation argument.
nodes.text_preview: [Multiplicative cancellation] Let $F$ be a field and let $a,b,c F$ with $c 0$. If \[ a c = b c, \] then $a = b$.

nodes.name: Uniqueness of multiplicative inverse
nodes.question: State the theorem: Uniqueness of multiplicative inverse.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $F$ be a field and let $a\in F$ with $a\neq 0$. If $b\in F$
satisfies $a\cdot b = 1$, then $b = a^{-1}$.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $F$ be a field and let $a\in F$ with $a\neq 0$. If $b\in F$
satisfies $a\cdot b = 1$, then $b = a^{-1}$.
nodes.proof_sketch:
\textbf{Professional Standard Proof.}~\\
Since $a\neq 0$ and $F$ is a field, the inverse $a^{-1}$ exists and satisfies
\[
a\cdot a^{-1}=1.
\]
Now compute:
\[
b=b\cdot 1=b\cdot(a\cdot a^{-1})=(b\cdot a)\cdot a^{-1}=(a\cdot b)\cdot a^{-1}=1\cdot a^{-1}=a^{-1},
\]
using associativity, commutativity, the hypothesis $a\cdot b=1$, and the
multiplicative identity axiom.
nodes.proof_idea:
The proof exhibits two right inverses of the same nonzero element $a$:
$b$ from the hypothesis and $a^{-1}$ from the field axiom.  Instead of
invoking cancellation, it inserts the identity $a\cdot a^{-1}=1$ and then
rewrites $b$ by associativity until the hypothesis $a\cdot b=1$ can be
substituted.  The conclusion falls out by a direct chain of equalities.
nodes.text_preview: [Uniqueness of multiplicative inverse] Let $F$ be a field and let $a F$ with $a 0$. If $b F$ satisfies $a b = 1$, then $b = a^ -1 $.

nodes.name: The inverse of one is one
nodes.question: State the theorem: The inverse of one is one.
nodes.statement_display:
In any field,
\[
1^{-1}=1.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
In any field,
\[
1^{-1}=1.
\]
nodes.proof_sketch:
Step 1. Recall the defining condition for a multiplicative inverse.

An element $y\in F$ is the multiplicative inverse of $x\in F\setminus\{0\}$
if and only if
\[
x\cdot y = 1.
\]
By uniqueness of multiplicative inverses
(\hyperref[thm:uniqueness-of-multiplicative-inverse]{Theorem~\ref*{thm:uniqueness-of-multiplicative-inverse}}),
there is exactly one such $y$, denoted $x^{-1}$.
Step 2. Verify that $1$ satisfies the defining condition for $1^{-1}$.

Compute:
\[
1\cdot 1 = 1.
\]
This uses the multiplicative identity axiom: $1$ is the identity element,
so $1\cdot 1 = 1$.
Step 3. Conclude by uniqueness.

The equation $1\cdot 1 = 1$ states that $1$ is a multiplicative inverse
of $1$.  By uniqueness of multiplicative inverses,
\[
1^{-1} = 1. \qedhere
\]
proof_steps:
Step 1. Recall the defining condition for a multiplicative inverse.

An element $y\in F$ is the multiplicative inverse of $x\in F\setminus\{0\}$
if and only if
\[
x\cdot y = 1.
\]
By uniqueness of multiplicative inverses
(\hyperref[thm:uniqueness-of-multiplicative-inverse]{Theorem~\ref*{thm:uniqueness-of-multiplicative-inverse}}),
there is exactly one such $y$, denoted $x^{-1}$.

Step 2. Verify that $1$ satisfies the defining condition for $1^{-1}$.

Compute:
\[
1\cdot 1 = 1.
\]
This uses the multiplicative identity axiom: $1$ is the identity element,
so $1\cdot 1 = 1$.

Step 3. Conclude by uniqueness.

The equation $1\cdot 1 = 1$ states that $1$ is a multiplicative inverse
of $1$.  By uniqueness of multiplicative inverses,
\[
1^{-1} = 1. \qedhere
\]
nodes.proof_idea:
The proof is a one-line uniqueness argument.  Exhibit $1$ as a solution to
$1\cdot y = 1$, which holds trivially by the multiplicative identity axiom.
Uniqueness of multiplicative inverses then pins down $1^{-1} = 1$.  No field
axiom beyond the multiplicative identity and uniqueness of inverses is
required.
